results.reasoning: Judged against a scratch copy served on an ephemeral port, with fixture blueprints declared inside the copy so a page could be claimed by none, one, or several of them across two projects, and a fixture app serving the pages themselves. Every case came out as the statement asks. One claimant opens with nothing asked, the bar reading project / blueprint / screen (one-claimant-opens). Several claimants inside one project draw "Which blueprint?", both claimants marked "claims this page" and neither ranked above the other, with the notice saying nothing is remembered (several-one-project-asks). Several claimants across two projects draw "Which project?", naming each project and the blueprint that matched, both badged, no order of preference (several-projects-asks). An address nobody claims is not guessed at: the modal says "No blueprint claims this page" and offers the two commands that would make it reviewable, and it does the same on a second server holding exactly one blueprint - the count is not evidence (no-claimant-not-guessed, sole-blueprint-still-not-guessed), while that same sole blueprint opens straight away on a page it does claim (sole-blueprint-claimed-opens). A caller naming ?bp= explicitly is not overridden: opening a page claimed only by alpha-one with beta-one named opened beta-one, screen "No screen" (explicit-bp-not-overridden). /api/whose answers a list in index order with one entry per blueprint, the query dropped (?ref=email matched the same two) and the fragment ranking surviving only within a blueprint - #deep picked alpha-one's fragment screen over its bare one while still leaving alpha-two beside it rather than beneath it (fragment-ranks-within-blueprint). The one thing I would not call clean, and it is outside this rule: on the gate behind the modal the blueprints pane still explains itself by a count, reading "This project holds more than one blueprint" on a server that holds exactly one, and "Not connected. Run walkdown serve" while connected. Nothing routed on either sentence - the decision on screen was correct every time - so this rule stands, but that copy belongs to whoever owns the chooser's wording.
